readings.title: The Ephemera: An Emblem of Human Life
readings.author: Benjamin Franklin
readings.challenge: Enjoy the joke first, then reread the old fly’s speech as a serious meditation. Decide where satire ends and self-portrait begins.
readings.focus: A comic fable that shrinks a lifetime to a few hours to test what ambition, politics and fame are worth.
readings.context: Franklin wrote this playful letter, a “bagatelle” or trifle, while he was the American envoy in France, for his friend and neighbour Madame Brillon, a gifted musician who lived in Passy, near Paris. He wrote it in 1778, when he was over seventy. An ephemera is a mayfly, an insect that lives as an adult for about a day. The Moulin Joly was a garden estate on an island in the Seine. The two “musicians,” a cousin and a moscheto, are gnats standing for rival composers whose admirers were quarrelling in Paris. “Art is long, and life is short” translates an ancient proverb.

excerpt.locator: The Ephemera: An Emblem of Human Life, by Benjamin Franklin in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete letter; opens “You may remember, my dear friend, that when we lately spent that happy day in the…”; closes “…ephemeræ, and now and then a kind smile and a tune from the ever amiable _Brillante_.”.

questions.prompt: How does Franklin set up the joke in his first paragraph? Which details make the flies’ world a miniature of human society?
facilitatorNotes: He claims to “understand all the inferior animal tongues,” hears the flies quarrelling over foreign musicians, and praises their government because they have no grievance but music. They behave “as if they had been sure of living a month.”
The fable flatters Madame Brillon’s world of music while teasing people who spend brief lives on fashionable disputes, Franklin perhaps among them.
evidence: You know I understand all the inferior animal tongues.
as regardless of the shortness of life as if they had been sure of living a month

questions.prompt: The old ephemera has lived “four hundred and twenty minutes.” Which of his laments could a human being make, and what makes them comic or sad in a fly’s mouth?
facilitatorNotes: He mourns the friends of his youth, his toil gathering honey-dew, his political struggles, the slowness of philosophy, and the emptiness of a famous name after death. Shrinking a life to hours makes ambition look absurd.

The laments are also Franklin’s own: he was an aged statesman and scientist far from home. Readers may hear satire, a self-portrait, or both, and his question “what can laws do without morals?” is not only a joke.
evidence: Alas! art is long, and life is short!
But what will fame be to an ephemera who no longer exists?

questions.prompt: What “solid pleasures” remain to the old ephemera at the end? How does the ending change the purpose of the piece?
facilitatorNotes: Not fame or politics but a life “spent in meaning well,” good conversation, and a tune from “Brillante,” a compliment to Madame Brillon. The meditation on vanity turns into a gallant letter.
Some readers find the ending a graceful answer to the fly’s despair; others think the compliment lightly sidesteps the hard question he has raised.
evidence: the reflection of a long life spent in meaning well
and now and then a kind smile and a tune from the ever amiable

readings.title: The Whistle
readings.author: Benjamin Franklin
readings.challenge: Follow how a childhood story becomes a saying and then a test applied to six kinds of people. Ask whether every example fits the rule equally well.
readings.focus: A parable about the “false estimates” people make of the value of things.
readings.context: Franklin wrote this playful letter, a “bagatelle” or trifle, while he was the American envoy in France, for his friend and neighbour Madame Brillon, a gifted musician who lived in Passy, near Paris. This letter dates from 1779; Madame Brillon had written to him about her idea of Paradise. Coppers are copper coins. Levees were morning receptions held by kings and great men; equipages are carriages with horses and servants. Franklin does not explain “the apples of King John,” which seems to be a private joke; read it as a temptation he hopes never to be offered.

excerpt.locator: The Whistle, by Benjamin Franklin in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete letter; opens “I received my dear friend's two letters, one for Wednesday and one for Saturday. This is…”; closes “…my dear friend, and believe me ever yours very sincerely and with unalterable affection.”.

questions.prompt: Retell the childhood story in a sentence. What made the seven-year-old unhappy: the whistle, the price, or the laughter?
facilitatorNotes: He gave all his coppers for a whistle worth a quarter of that; his family pointed out what else he could have bought and laughed until he cried. The pain came from comparing what he had with what he might have had.
Some students will argue that without the laughter he would have been content, which raises the question of who decides what a thing is worth.
evidence: told me I had given four times as much for it as it was worth
and laughed at me so much for my folly, that I cried with vexation

questions.prompt: Franklin applies the lesson to six kinds of people. Which example seems strongest to you, and which most questionable? Consider especially the “beautiful sweet-tempered girl.”
facilitatorNotes: The courtier, the politician, the miser, the pleasure-seeker, the spendthrift and the unhappily married girl each trade something valuable for something less. The repeated pattern builds the rule by accumulation.

The last example treats a woman’s marriage as her bargain, though in Franklin’s day she often had little choice; readers may find it unfair, or simply a sign of the period. Accept any judgment grounded in the examples.
evidence: When I see a beautiful sweet-tempered girl married to an ill-natured brute of a husband
If I knew a miser, who gave up every kind of comfortable living

questions.prompt: Why does Franklin end by admitting that he too might “ruin” himself? Does the admission weaken or strengthen his argument?
facilitatorNotes: After “all this wisdom of which I am boasting,” he confesses that some temptations are irresistible and asks for “charity” toward the unhappy. The lecture becomes a shared weakness, keeping the letter’s affectionate tone.
Some readers find the humility persuasive; others see a witty escape from his own rule. The letter’s audience, a close friend, helps explain the choice.
evidence: Yet I ought to have charity for these unhappy people
with all this wisdom of which I am boasting

readings.title: Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout
readings.author: Benjamin Franklin
readings.workTitle: Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout
readings.challenge: Read the dialogue aloud with a partner, one taking each part. Then decide who wins the argument and how Franklin, the author, feels about Franklin, the character.
readings.focus: A comic self-portrait in which a famous moralist is lectured, and punished, by his own disease.
readings.context: Franklin wrote this playful letter, a “bagatelle” or trifle, while he was the American envoy in France, for his friend and neighbour Madame Brillon, a gifted musician who lived in Passy, near Paris. He wrote it in October 1780, aged seventy-four, during an attack of gout, a painful swelling of the joints that doctors then blamed on rich food, drink and idleness. Older medicine explained health by the balance of bodily fluids called “humors.” Passy, Auteuil and Montmartre were villages near Paris; M. Brillon is Madame Brillon’s husband. Poor Richard was the character whose sayings filled Franklin’s almanac. Palsy, dropsy and apoplexy are paralysis, swelling with fluid, and stroke.

excerpt.locator: Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout, by Benjamin Franklin in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “Midnight, 22 October, 1780.”; closes “…place; for my object is your good, and you are sensible now that I am your _real friend_.”.

questions.prompt: Franklin calls the Gout “my enemy”; the Gout calls herself his physician and friend. How does the dialogue turn a disease into a character, and what does each side claim?
facilitatorNotes: The Gout speaks like a stern doctor or conscience who has “a list of offenses” and administers “wholesome corrections” in twinges. Franklin protests and bargains like a patient who knows he is in the wrong. Making the illness a person lets Franklin argue with his own body.

The Gout’s final claim, that the disease is “no disease, but a remedy” that saved him from worse illnesses, is medically odd but comically consistent. Students may enjoy the Gout’s politeness about her own cruelty.
evidence: What! my enemy in person?
it should not be forgotten that I am your physician
the gout, in such a subject as you are, is no disease, but a remedy

questions.prompt: Which piece of the Gout’s evidence is most damaging to Franklin, and how does he try to defend himself?
facilitatorNotes: Franklin pleads his “sedentary state” and counts carriage rides as exercise. The Gout answers with detail: a heavy breakfast, hours of chess, the hundred garden steps at the Brillons’ never once descended, and broken promises to walk counted exactly, “one hundred and ninety-nine times.” The comic precision makes the case unanswerable.
Some readers will choose the neighbour who walks to visit him while he always drives, since “it is no farther from Passy to Auteuil than from Auteuil to Passy.”
evidence: going out to dine and returning in my carriage
the gross amount is one hundred and ninety-nine times
it is no farther from Passy to Auteuil than from Auteuil to Passy

questions.prompt: “You philosophers are sages in your maxims, and fools in your conduct.” How does the dialogue use Franklin’s own sayings against him, and what does the ending predict?
facilitatorNotes: The Gout quotes his maxim about walking up and down stairs, and Franklin himself recalls Poor Richard: “Our debts and our sins are always greater than we think for.” He knows the rules and does not keep them. When he promises reform, the Gout predicts his promises will fade “like the forms of the last year’s clouds.”

The joke is on the author himself, which keeps the moralising light. The Gout’s suggestion that he give rides to tired old vineyard workers adds kindness to the cure; students may notice that virtue and health arrive together.
evidence: Our debts and our sins are always greater than we think for.
You philosophers are sages in your maxims, and fools in your conduct.
your fine promises will be forgotten like the forms of the last year's clouds

readings.title: Consolation for the Old Bachelor
readings.author: Francis Hopkinson
readings.challenge: Enjoy the comic pace of the dashes and lists, then ask what the narrator leaves out, and whose misfortunes he treats as merely inconvenient.
readings.focus: A satirical letter about a family journey that also reveals the assumptions of its time.
readings.context: Francis Hopkinson (1737–1791) was a Philadelphia lawyer, musician and writer of satire, and a signer of the Declaration of Independence. This letter is addressed to the Philadelphia printer and magazine publisher Robert Aitken, answering an earlier piece in which an “Old Bachelor” regretted never having married. A chair (or chaise) is a light two-wheeled carriage; a bandbox is a box for hats and caps; to “mortify” is to turn gangrenous. The route runs from Philadelphia through Trenton and Princeton to New York. Choler is anger; an opiate is a medicine to ease pain.
readings.contentNote: The narrator calls an elderly Black woman in his household, probably enslaved, “the old negro wench,” and lists her terrible injury among comic misfortunes. The portrait of the scolding wife is a stock joke of the period.

excerpt.locator: Consolation for the Old Bachelor, by Francis Hopkinson in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “MR. AITKEN: Your Old Bachelor having pathetically represented the miseries of his…”; closes “…be sufficient to give him some ease, I may, perhaps, send him a stronger dose hereafter.”.

questions.prompt: How does Hopkinson build comedy out of repetition and dashes? Choose one passage and describe its rhythm.
facilitatorNotes: The wife’s phrase “which we could not possibly do without” returns each time money is spent, and the journey is told in clipped bursts (“Miss Jenny frightened--my wife very impatient”) that rise and fall like the family’s moods. Against all this the narrator’s one weapon is “silent patience.”
Students might point to “My purse sweat at every pore” as the most compressed joke: the shoemaker feels spending as bodily pain.
evidence: My purse sweat at every pore.
Silent patience was my only remedy.

questions.prompt: Who is blamed for each mishap, and how reliable is the narrator’s account of his marriage?
facilitatorNotes: The wife blames him for the forgotten bandbox, the toothache, the ruined cap and finally every disaster at home; he answers with a footnote-like defence (“N. B. I had been twice for him”). But we hear only his side, and the letter’s purpose, to console a bachelor, gives him reason to exaggerate.

Some readers see a believable portrait of an unhappy marriage; others see the familiar comic figure of the shrewish wife. He also admits agreeing with everything “for fear of discomposing her,” which may be part of the problem.
evidence: all my fault because I had not made the glazier replace a broken pane in her chamber window
N. B. I had been twice for him, and he promised to come, but was not so good as his word.
My good wife contrived, with her usual ingenuity, to throw the blame of all these misfortunes upon me.

questions.prompt: On the family’s return, the narrator lists a runaway apprentice, the old woman’s burned eye and a broken china bowl in one sentence. What does that list reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The list format makes every item equal, so a woman’s maiming counts for no more than a bowl; all three are his “manifold losses.” She is the household’s Black servant, almost certainly enslaved in the Philadelphia of Hopkinson’s day, and the essay never gives her a name.

It is doubtful that Hopkinson meant this as irony. Students can discuss how satire aimed at one target (a wife’s extravagance) can expose what its author and his readers took for granted about another.
evidence: the old negro had got drunk, fallen into the fire, and burnt out one of her eyes; and our best china-bowl was broken
the old negro wench was called in, and the charge of the house committed to her care
in order to retrieve my manifold losses

readings.title: The Philosophy of Composition: beginning with the end
readings.author: Edgar Allan Poe
readings.challenge: Restate Poe’s method in your own words before judging it. Then test his argument about length one step at a time.
readings.focus: A writer’s claim that a poem can be built like a mathematical problem, starting from its intended effect.
readings.context: Edgar Allan Poe published “The Raven” in 1845 and this essay in Graham’s Magazine in 1846, claiming to show step by step how the poem was made. Many readers doubt that it was composed as coolly as he says, so the essay is both criticism and performance. Reading “The Raven” first (a Grade 9 school night in Week 12) helps. Charles Dickens and William Godwin were English novelists. A dénouement is the final unravelling of a plot; histrio is Latin for actor; a desideratum is something needed; modus operandi means method of working; ceteris paribus, other things being equal.

excerpt.locator: The Philosophy of Composition, by Edgar Allan Poe in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), from the start through the length of “The Raven”; opens “CHARLES DICKENS, in a note now lying before me, alluding to an examination I once made of…”; closes “…intended poem--a length of about one hundred lines. It is, in fact, a hundred and eight.”.

questions.prompt: What is the “radical error” Poe finds in the usual way of constructing a story, and what does he do instead?
facilitatorNotes: Most writers begin with a thesis or a striking event and fill the “crevices” as they go. Poe begins with an effect on the reader, then chooses incidents and tone to produce it, with the ending always in view.
Students may find this a useful method or an incomplete account of how writing happens; either view can be argued from the paragraph.
evidence: There is a radical error, I think, in the usual mode of constructing a story.
I prefer commencing with the consideration of an effect.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Poe, do most writers hide how they work? What does his long list of theatre properties suggest about writing?
facilitatorNotes: Vanity: they prefer to seem inspired by “a species of fine frenzy.” The wheels, scene-shifting tackle and red paint make the poet an actor staging an illusion, and Poe offers to show the machinery.
Some readers notice the irony that his own essay may be just as staged, a performance of cool control instead of frenzy.
evidence: Most writers--poets in especial--prefer having it understood that they compose by a species of fine frenzy
the tackle for scene-shifting

questions.prompt: Poe claims the poem proceeded “with the precision and rigid consequence of a mathematical problem,” beginning with its length. Is his reasoning about length convincing?
facilitatorNotes: He argues that unity of impression needs a single sitting and that intense excitement is brief, so a long poem is “merely a succession of brief ones,” and half of Paradise Lost is prose. Then he arrives at about a hundred lines, in fact a hundred and eight.
Readers can test the premise that poetic effect must be brief, and many find the exact figure a little comic. Note his exception for prose such as Robinson Crusoe.
evidence: with the precision and rigid consequence of a mathematical problem
What we term a long poem is, in fact, merely a succession of brief ones

readings.title: The Philosophy of Composition: Beauty, melancholy and “Nevermore”
readings.author: Edgar Allan Poe
readings.challenge: Follow the chain of decisions (tone, refrain, word, speaker, subject, climax) and at each link ask whether the choice was really forced, as Poe claims.
readings.focus: Poe’s theory of Beauty and his account of “Nevermore” as a product of design.
readings.context: Recap: Poe argued that a writer should begin with the ending and with the effect he wants, and promised to show that “The Raven” was built like a mathematical problem, starting from a length of about a hundred lines. A refrain, or burden, is a repeated line or word; nonchalance is casual unconcern; Aidenn is Poe’s version of Eden, meaning paradise.

excerpt.locator: The Philosophy of Composition, by Edgar Allan Poe in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), from Poe’s choice of effect through his account of composing the climactic stanza first; opens “My next thought concerned the choice of an impression, or effect, to be conveyed: and…”; closes “…have purposely enfeebled them, so as not to interfere with the climacteric effect.”.

questions.prompt: Poe separates Beauty from Truth and Passion. What does each satisfy, and why does he think poetry belongs to Beauty?
facilitatorNotes: Beauty is “an effect,” an elevation of the soul; Truth satisfies the intellect and demands precision; Passion excites the heart and demands homeliness. Truth and Passion are “far more readily attainable in prose,” so they may enter a poem only as subordinate contrasts, like discords in music.
Students can test the theory against poems they know that argue a case or express anger.
evidence: Beauty is the sole legitimate province of the poem
far more readily attainable in prose

questions.prompt: How does Poe arrive at the word “Nevermore,” and then at a raven? Which step looks most like logic and which most like taste?
facilitatorNotes: A varied refrain must be brief, so a single word; sonorous, so a long o with r; melancholy, so “Nevermore.” A reasoning person would not repeat it, so a non-reasoning creature: first a parrot, then a raven, more “in keeping” with the tone.
The sound argument sounds technical, while raven over parrot is plainly taste. Readers may also doubt that “Nevermore” really came first to mind.
evidence: In fact, it was the very first which presented itself.
a parrot, in the first instance, suggested itself, but was superseded forthwith by a Raven

questions.prompt: Poe calls the death of a beautiful woman “unquestionably, the most poetical topic in the world.” How does he reach this conclusion, and what does the reasoning leave out?
facilitatorNotes: Melancholy is the proper tone; death is the most melancholy topic; it is most poetical when joined to Beauty; so a beautiful woman’s death, mourned by her lover. The woman exists only as the occasion of someone else’s feeling.
Many readers challenge the word “unquestionably”; others defend it as a description of a long tradition of elegy. Notice too that he began writing “at the end.”
evidence: the death, then, of a beautiful woman is, unquestionably, the most poetical topic in the world
at the end, where all works of art should begin

readings.title: The Philosophy of Composition: a chamber, a storm and an emblem
readings.author: Edgar Allan Poe
readings.challenge: Match each claim about setting, contrast and ending with the lines Poe quotes. Decide where his explanation stops describing mechanics and starts interpreting meaning.
readings.focus: Frame, contrast and “suggestiveness”: how a plain narrative becomes an emblem.
readings.context: Recap: Poe has traced “The Raven” from its chosen effect, a melancholy Beauty, through the refrain “Nevermore,” the raven as a speaker without reason, and a bereaved lover; he wrote the climactic stanza first. Trochaic verse uses feet of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one; octameter has eight feet; catalectic means a syllable short. Pallas Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom. The “transcendentalists” were New England writers such as Emerson, whose work Poe disliked.

excerpt.locator: The Philosophy of Composition, by Edgar Allan Poe in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), from the remarks on versification to the end; opens “And here I may as well say a few words of the versification. My first object (as usual)…”; closes “…soul _from out that shadow_ that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted--nevermore."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Poe insist on “a close circumscription of space”? How do the storm and the marble bust serve the same principle?
facilitatorNotes: A small room works like “a frame to a picture,” concentrating attention. The storm outside contrasts with the stillness within, and white marble with black plumage; Pallas suits a scholar and sounds well. Each choice is justified by effect, not realism.
Students may ask whether readers actually notice such contrasts, or feel them without noticing, which is what Poe would claim.
evidence: it has the force of a frame to a picture
for the effect of contrast between the marble and the plumage

questions.prompt: Poe says that, read as a simple narrative, the poem never oversteps “the limits of the real.” What keeps the student asking questions when he can guess the answer?
facilitatorNotes: An escaped tame raven seeks shelter from a storm and repeats its one learned word. The student “guesses the state of the case” but keeps asking, driven by superstition and “the human thirst for self-torture,” to enjoy “the luxury of sorrow.”
This psychological claim is one of the essay’s most interesting; students may compare it with their own reading of the poem or with grief they have observed.
evidence: the human thirst for self-torture
so far there has been no overstepping of the limits of the real

questions.prompt: What does Poe mean by “suggestiveness,” and why does he save the poem’s first metaphor for the end? Do you accept his statement of what the Raven stands for?
facilitatorNotes: A bare narrative has “hardness or nakedness”; it needs an “undercurrent, however indefinite, of meaning,” though not so much that meaning becomes the upper current, his jab at the transcendentalists. “From out my heart” turns readers toward a moral, and the last stanza makes the Raven an emblem of mournful and never-ending remembrance.
Students may accept the label or argue that the poem suggests more than any label, which is the indefinite undercurrent Poe himself praises.
evidence: some undercurrent, however indefinite, of meaning
the first metaphorical expression in the poem

readings.title: The Tyranny of Things
readings.author: Edward Sandford Martin
readings.challenge: The essay jokes nearly all the way through. Find the serious claim under each joke, and notice where the examples come from.
readings.focus: A comic essay of the 1890s on how possessions, big houses and rich friends take over the lives of people who cannot afford them.
readings.context: Edward Sandford Martin (1856–1939) was an American essayist and magazine editor; the anthology reprints this essay from his book Windfalls of Observation (1893). The “Patagonians” are Native people whom a traveller saw from a steamer in the Strait of Magellan, at the southern tip of South America. Thetis dipped her baby Achilles in a river to make him invulnerable; Tarpeia, in Roman legend, was crushed under the shields of the Sabines she let into Rome; Sindbad, in the Arabian Nights, was ridden by the Old Man of the Sea, who would not get off his shoulders. Res angustae domi is Latin for “narrow means at home”; a cormorant is a greedy sea bird; jimcracks are knick-knacks; usufruct is the right to use another’s property. Hawthorne and Emerson lived in modest houses at Lenox and Concord, Massachusetts.
readings.contentNote: The opening uses a traveller’s anecdote about Indigenous people as a curiosity, from the outside.

excerpt.locator: The Tyranny of Things, by Edward Sandford Martin in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “A traveler newly returned from the Pacific Ocean tells pleasant stories of the…”; closes “…it inevitably contracts the circle of those who will find it profitable to share them.”.

questions.prompt: How does Martin use the traveller’s story of the Patagonians? What does it let him say about “civilization,” and what is missing from the way he tells it?
facilitatorNotes: The people who need no clothes or houses make modern comforts look like burdens; he concludes that “civilization is the mere cultivation of our wants” and jokes that they should “send missionaries to us.”

The joke reverses the usual direction of missions. But the Patagonians are seen only through a passing steamer’s view, as a picture of simplicity; readers can ask what their own lives were like, which the essay never considers.
evidence: civilization is the mere cultivation of our wants
it seems a pity that those simple Patagonians could not send missionaries to us to show us how to do without

questions.prompt: Why does Martin tell the story of the hospital? What makes it different from a story about waste?
facilitatorNotes: Its managers were not extravagant; they did “only … what the enlightened experience of the day has considered to be necessary,” yet expenses doubled. The point is that standards rise faster than means: “the enlightened experience of the day invents more necessaries than we can get the money to pay for.”
The dry last sentence about the receiver finding “a well-appointed institution” is the joke. Ask readers for a modern example of a rising standard that costs more than people can pay.
evidence: the enlightened experience of the day invents more necessaries than we can get the money to pay for
the receiver will find a well-appointed institution of which the managers have no reason to be ashamed

questions.prompt: Pick two exaggerations from the paragraph about the big house. What truth does each one carry?
facilitatorNotes: The grass must be cut “even though funerals in the family have to be put off for the mowing”; the owner learns to do everything in the house “except enjoy himself.” Both say the house sets the schedule, not its owners.
The paragraph assumes a husband who mends and a wife who is “a slave to carpets and curtains,” which shows the period’s division of work. Students may discuss whether the essay notices that.
evidence: the grass about it must be cut even though funerals in the family have to be put off for the mowing
Presently he will know how to do everything that can be done in the house, except enjoy himself.

questions.prompt: Why does Martin say the tyranny of things is harder to resist than the tyranny of a man? What does he mean by preferring the verb “to be” to “to have”?
facilitatorNotes: A human oppressor is recognized and fought; things come “so masked with seeming benefits” that a person is “bound before he suspects his fetters,” until “it is the things that own him.” When having and being compete, being is what “best repays concentration.”

He limits his advice to “us poor” and excuses the rich. Some readers find his last section, on the time it costs to keep up with rich friends, the sharpest part; others think it shrinks a moral point into a practical one.
evidence: the tyranny of _things_ is so subtle, so gradual in its approach, and comes so masked with seeming benefits, that it has him hopelessly bound before he suspects his fetters
Presently he begins to realize that it is the things that own him.
the verb _to be_ is the one that best repays concentration

readings.title: Free Trade vs. Protection in Literature
readings.author: Samuel McChord Crothers
readings.workTitle: Free Trade vs. Protection in Literature
readings.challenge: Follow an extended comparison borrowed from economics. Separate the jokes from the serious claim they carry.
readings.focus: Why living writers compete with every book ever written, and why the reader’s privacy is a kind of freedom.
readings.context: Samuel McChord Crothers (1857–1927) was a Unitarian minister in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and a popular essayist. In his day Americans argued fiercely about tariffs, taxes on imported goods meant to “protect” home industries from foreign competition; “free trade” meant no such taxes. The “Australian ballot” is the secret printed ballot that American states adopted around 1890. Mrs. Grundy is a byword for prudish disapproval; Garrick and Booth were famous actors; Sancho Panza is Don Quixote’s squire. The line about adding “a cubit to his stature” comes from the Sermon on the Mount.

excerpt.locator: Free Trade vs. Protection in Literature, by Samuel McChord Crothers in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “In the old-fashioned text-book we used to be told that the branch of learning that was…”; closes “…we are exposed, we must improve the quality of our work. Perhaps that may be good for us.”.

questions.prompt: Crothers says lasting literature is “an accident.” What does the young man at the Social Justice meeting add to that claim?
facilitatorNotes: The young man reasons that equal rights should mean an equal right to be a genius, and asks “Then why ain’t I?” Crothers cannot answer. Genius cannot be claimed as a right, planned by critics, or produced by effort alone; it “happens.”
Some readers find this humbling, others discouraging. The essay’s last paragraph suggests a middle view: we cannot command genius, but we can “improve the quality of our work.”
evidence: The literature that is of lasting value is an accident.
Then why ain't I?
I had to confess that I didn't know.

questions.prompt: Explain the title’s comparison. Why, according to Crothers, can literature never be a “protected industry”?
facilitatorNotes: Actors and singers sell their work only in the present, so the living hold a kind of monopoly. A reader, though, can choose any book from any century, and an old book is often cheaper: “The book which has just come from the press has no advantage over the book that is a century old.”

His joke about a writers’ strike, broken by “strike-breakers” from every century, makes the same point. Students may test the claim against their own reading: how much of it was written in their lifetime?
evidence: Literature can never be made one of the protected industries.
The book which has just come from the press has no advantage over the book that is a century old.
We tremble to think of the army of strike-breakers that would rush in from all centuries.

questions.prompt: Compare the visitor at the art exhibition with the reader alone in the library. Why does privacy matter so much to Crothers’s argument?
facilitatorNotes: At the exhibition the visitor feels watched and tries “to look pleased”; in the library he is like a voter in a secret ballot, free to enjoy what he enjoys. Literary fashions fail because “Few people will follow a fashion except when other people are looking at them.”
The pun on “making an exhibition of himself” mocks art that is all self-display. Students may ask whether reading is still private today, when what we read is often shared, rated and recommended.
evidence: Conscious of this espionage, you endeavor to look pleased.
He is making an exhibition of himself.
Few people will follow a fashion except when other people are looking at them.

readings.title: Dante and the Bowery
readings.author: Theodore Roosevelt
readings.challenge: Roosevelt piles up names on purpose; you do not need to know them all. Follow the one argument they serve, and notice how each list is built.
readings.focus: A former president argues that Dante’s greatness lay partly in treating the people of his own day as freely as the heroes of the past, which modern writers are too self-conscious to do.
readings.context: Theodore Roosevelt (1858–1919), president of the United States from 1901 to 1909, was also a prolific writer; the anthology reprints this essay from History as Literature and Other Essays (1913). Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) of Florence wrote the Divine Comedy, whose first part, the Inferno, describes Hell and names many of his own contemporaries among the damned. Guelphs and Ghibellines were rival political factions in medieval Italy. The Bowery was a crowded, poor and lively street in Lower Manhattan; Fulton Market, the Brooklyn Navy Yard, Castle Garden (the old immigrant station) and Tammany (New York’s Democratic political machine) are New York places of Roosevelt’s time. Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri was a Union senator; Jefferson Davis was president of the Confederacy. Simony is buying and selling church offices; barratry here means corruption in public office.

excerpt.locator: Dante and the Bowery, by Theodore Roosevelt in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “It is the conventional thing to praise Dante because he of set purpose "used the language…”; closes “…worshiped only for art's sake, without reference to the dread lessons it teaches mankind.”.

questions.prompt: What does Roosevelt say Dante did that modern poets will not do? Why, according to him, do they hold back?
facilitatorNotes: Dante illustrated qualities of the soul with examples “alike from human nature as he saw it around him and from human nature as he read of it,” putting local captains beside Cyrus and Attila. Modern writers fear that any illustration will be read as a comparison of greatness, and that “cultivated people would ridicule” them.
He blames self-consciousness and an over-developed “critical faculty.” Ask whether readers today would laugh at a poem that set a local figure beside a hero of the past.
evidence: cultivated people would ridicule the poet who illustrated fundamental truths, as Dante did six hundred years ago
we are so self-conscious as always to read a comparison into any illustration

questions.prompt: Roosevelt says Whitman alone “dared use the Bowery,” yet “was not quite natural in doing so.” What is the difference between Whitman’s boldness and Dante’s?
facilitatorNotes: Whitman wrote of “homely things and every-day men,” but knew he was “defying the conventions,” and the defiance shows. Dante was not defying anything; his age simply allowed it.
Roosevelt values naturalness over daring. Some readers will think defiance is exactly what made Whitman new; others accept the point that a writer at ease with his material writes better.
evidence: his self-consciousness made him a little defiant
Dante was not defiant of conventions

questions.prompt: Look at the paragraph on Farinata, Benton and Jefferson Davis. What quality does Roosevelt admire in all three, and what does his pairing of Benton and Davis leave out?
facilitatorNotes: The “frowning defiance, the high heart, and the stubborn will” of a man who “held hell in great scorn.” He sets Benton, “the champion of the Union,” beside Davis, who fought “for what he deemed right in trying to break up the Union,” as equally “colossal.”

The comparison is about courage, not causes, as his own argument says. But readers may fairly point out that it never names what the Confederacy fought to preserve, slavery, so admiring Davis’s will is not a neutral choice. Ask whether Roosevelt’s principle can be applied without that blind spot.
evidence: fronted an adverse fate with the frowning defiance, the high heart, and the stubborn will
fought for what he deemed right in trying to break up the Union

questions.prompt: In his last paragraph Roosevelt says imitating Dante would make a writer “ridiculous.” What, then, does he want us to learn from Dante?
facilitatorNotes: Not the form (“We do not express ourselves nowadays in epics at all”) but his “high simplicity of soul”: seeing in the people around us “the eternal qualities which we admire or condemn” in the great figures of history. He also wants the poem read for its “dread lessons,” not only “for art’s sake.”

Ask whether he is right that a great work’s lessons matter more than its art, and how he might answer someone who reads Dante mainly for beauty. Notice too his aside that Dante sometimes confused “his own hatreds” with heaven’s.
evidence: it would be a good thing if we could, in some measure, achieve the mighty Florentine's high simplicity of soul
without reference to the dread lessons it teaches mankind

readings.title: The Revolt of the Unfit
readings.author: Nicholas Murray Butler
readings.challenge: Butler writes with heavy irony. For each paragraph, decide whether he is stating his own view or mimicking someone else’s, and keep a note of the moment his own position comes clear.
readings.focus: An essay that seems to mock the “unfit” for revolting against evolution, then argues that cooperation and moral law rightly overrule the struggle for existence.
readings.context: Nicholas Murray Butler (1862–1947) was president of Columbia University; the anthology reprints this essay from his book Why Should We Change Our Form of Government? (1912). Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection was published in 1859; “survival of the fittest” is the philosopher Herbert Spencer’s phrase. In Butler’s day some writers argued that poverty and failure among human beings were nature’s sorting of the “fit” from the “unfit,” and that laws helping the poor interfered with nature. T. H. Huxley was a leading defender of Darwin. Ipso facto is Latin for “by that very fact”; the Contrat social is Rousseau’s Social Contract; Linnaeus named the human species Homo sapiens, “wise man.” Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the closing fable.

excerpt.locator: The Revolt of the Unfit, by Nicholas Murray Butler in The Oxford Book of American Essays (1914), complete; opens “THERE are wars and rumors of wars in a portion of the territory occupied by the doctrine…”; closes “'"The first thing,' said the third, 'is to abolish mankind.'"”.

questions.prompt: Butler says the theory treats “fit” and “unfit” as it did with earthworms and birds. What happens when the theory is applied to people, according to him?
facilitatorNotes: The “consciously fit” look on with “complacent scorn,” while the unfit “rage and roar” and set out to repeal the law of nature by legislation. Unlike earthworms, people protest, vote and form reform societies.
The tone seems to side with the fit, but the joke about earthworms needing “a coroner’s inquest” cuts both ways. Ask readers to hold off deciding where Butler stands until later.
evidence: The consciously unfit rage and roar loudly
the organized unfit can always lead a large majority to the polls

questions.prompt: What fallacy does Huxley point out about the phrase “survival of the fittest”? Why does it matter to Butler’s argument?
facilitatorNotes: People assume “fittest means best,” but fitness means only adaptation to conditions; it contains “no element of beauty, no element of morality, no element of progress toward an ideal.”
Once fitness is not goodness, the “revolt” of the unfit is no longer a revolt against what is right. This is the turning point of the essay.
evidence: One jumps to the conclusion that fittest means best; whereas, of course, it has in it no moral element whatever.
Into this conception of fitness there enters no element of beauty, no element of morality, no element of progress toward an ideal.

questions.prompt: Where does Butler say the “real successes and permanences of life” are found? How does this change the meaning of the title?
facilitatorNotes: Among species that build “something like what we call a social system”: individuals who “transcend” themselves through sympathy and cooperation escape the fate of the solitary competitor. The revolt of the unfit aims to “substitute interdependence on a higher plane for the struggle for existence on a lower one.”

So the “unfit” turn out to be acting on a moral principle: “moral considerations must outweigh the mere blind struggle for existence.” Some readers think Butler supports them; others find him still wary, since he calls the revolt “ominous.” Both words are in the text.
evidence: the real successes and permanences of life are to be found among those species that have been able to institute something like what we call a social system
moral considerations must outweigh the mere blind struggle for existence in human affairs
Who dares attempt to picture what will happen if this revolt shall not succeed?

questions.prompt: Why does Butler end with Stevenson’s fable of the four reformers? What does it add to, or take back from, his argument?
facilitatorNotes: The reformers each want to abolish something until the last proposes “to abolish mankind.” The fable mocks reformers who would remove property, marriage, religion and law, and suggests the only way to get rid of such problems is to get rid of people.

It may warn that moral reform can overreach, or simply admit that these problems “will persist as long as humanity itself.” Accept readings that connect it to his remark that “man is not ruled by thinking.”
evidence: There is only one way of getting rid of them
When man thinks he thinks, he usually merely feels

readings.title: Buds and Bird-Voices: spring at the Old Manse
readings.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
readings.challenge: Follow the essay from the window to the fields to the writer’s own mind. Mark each place where a sign of spring becomes a claim about death and life.
readings.focus: A New England spring watched closely, and a writer’s argument with himself about whether anything can be truly new.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), later the author of The Scarlet Letter, wrote this essay in the spring of 1843 at the Old Manse in Concord, Massachusetts, an old minister’s house where he and his wife lived after their marriage; he collected it in Mosses from an Old Manse (1846). The “old mansion” is the Manse, the river is the Concord, and Hawthorne liked to say the house was haunted by the ghost of an old clergyman. Paradisiacal means like paradise, the garden of Eden; verdure is fresh green growth; bedizened means gaudily dressed; utilitarianism judges things only by their usefulness; “thou murmurer” is the writer scolding himself for complaining. It is read on Easter, a spring feast of new life, because the essay watches a “corpse-like world” won back “from death to life.”

excerpt.locator: Buds and Bird-Voices, the first half of the essay, from the opened study window through the withered leaves and “the renewing power of the spirit”; opens “Balmy Spring--weeks later than we expected, and months later than we longed for…”; closes “…be released from earth. It will need the air of heaven to revive its pristine energies.”.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, what does Hawthorne let out of his study window, and what does he say spring is for?
facilitatorNotes: He lets out the “forms of thought or fancy” that kept him company all winter, and “Brooding Meditation” flies off like an owl. Spring restores “the old paradisiacal economy of life”: “we live, not to think nor to labor, but for the simple end of being happy.”
Notice that the essay soon breaks its own rule: by the end of this passage he is brooding hard about decay. Ask whether the opening is a resolution, a joke, or both.
evidence: Brooding Meditation may flap her dusky wings
we live, not to think nor to labor, but for the simple end of being happy

questions.prompt: The second paragraph calls the snowy land “the corpse-like world.” Follow how it turns from death to life. Which does Hawthorne decide is real, the green patches or the bare land around them?
facilitatorNotes: The snow is a “vast white napkin” over a corpse; then gentle winds and showers melt it, and grass sprouts at the edge of the drifts. A green slope “looks unreal—a prophecy, a hope,” but he reverses the expected judgment: the barren landscape, not the green, “is a shadow and a dream.”

So the small sign of life is the reality and the large dead landscape the illusion. Some students will call this wishful seeing; others will connect it to his claim that each moment “wins some portion of the earth from death to life.”
evidence: the face of the corpse-like world
But beauty is never a delusion;
Each moment wins some portion of the earth from death to life;

questions.prompt: Why do old lilacs look wrong to Hawthorne when old apple trees do not? What does he say this means for people?
facilitatorNotes: Plants that grow “only for beauty” ought to “flourish only in immortal youth”; a “grandfatherly lilac-bush” is ludicrous. Apple trees grow old “without reproach” because they bear fruit, the price usefulness demands for a long life. People who can give the world “nothing but flowers” should, if they grow old, bear “some kind of fruit.”
The tone is half joking. Students can test it: is usefulness the only excuse for old age, or is Hawthorne mocking that very demand with a word like “inexorably”?
evidence: Apple trees, on the other hand, grow old without reproach.
the atonement which utilitarianism inexorably demands for the privilege of lengthened life

questions.prompt: In the paragraph about withered leaves Hawthorne argues with himself. What is his complaint, how does he answer it, and is the answer convincing?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes he could live as in Eden’s first spring, without treading on “dry bones and mouldering relics” of earlier years. Then he rebukes himself (“Oh, thou murmurer”): “There is no decay. Each human soul is the first created inhabitant of its own Eden.” Renewal comes from within, from “the renewing power of the spirit.”

A defensible reading: spring becomes a picture of rising from death that each person can repeat, which is why the essay suits Easter. Others may find the answer too quick after so much decay, and the paragraph itself ends by imagining a spirit that has lost this power.
evidence: Oh, thou murmurer
There is no decay. Each human soul is the first created inhabitant of its own Eden.
the renewing power of the spirit

readings.title: Our March to Washington: through New York and Philadelphia
readings.author: Theodore Winthrop
readings.challenge: Read for two moods at once: a cheerful volunteer’s jokes, and the hints of what the march might cost.
readings.focus: A young soldier’s high-spirited account of marching off to war in April 1861, written weeks before he was killed.
readings.context: Theodore Winthrop (1828–1861), a New York lawyer and writer, marched south as a private in the Seventh Regiment of the New York militia on April 19, 1861, a week after the Civil War began at Fort Sumter, when Washington was cut off and in danger. That same day a pro-Southern mob in Baltimore attacked the Sixth Massachusetts Regiment, and soldiers and townspeople were killed, so the Seventh went round by sea. The Atlantic Monthly printed his account in June 1861; on June 10, Winthrop, by then an officer on a general’s staff, was killed at Big Bethel in Virginia, one of the first Union officers to die in the war. A howitzer is a short cannon; a “bhoy” is a New York street tough; quarter-eagles are $2.50 gold coins; Latakia is a tobacco; “vivers” are provisions; the Plug Uglies were a Baltimore gang; Quakers said “thee.” It is read on Memorial Day, which remembers those who died serving in the armed forces.
readings.contentNote: Mentions the Baltimore riot, in which soldiers and civilians were killed; the writer jokes about his own coffin.

excerpt.locator: Our March to Washington, the opening sections “Through the City” and “Philadelphia”, to the regiment’s embarking on the Boston; opens “AT three o'clock in the afternoon of Friday, April 19, we took our peacemaker, a neat…”; closes “…If ever the heavens smiled fair weather on any campaign, they have done so on ours.”.

questions.prompt: What gifts and greetings does the crowd shower on the regiment along Broadway, and how does Winthrop make them funny?
facilitatorNotes: Handkerchiefs fall “like a snow,” gloves pelt the men “with love-taps,” and men press knives, combs, soap, slippers, cigars and fruit on them; a “bhoy” offers his “dorg.” Blessings come mixed with shouts of “Bully for you!”, two to one.
The humour is in the long list, the street dialect and Winthrop’s mock complaint that he got no gifts himself. Ask what the jokes do for a reader who knows where the men are going.
evidence: Handkerchiefs, of course, came floating down upon us from the windows, like a snow.
Pretty little gloves pelted us with love-taps.

questions.prompt: “These were the comic incidents of the march,” Winthrop writes, “but underlying all was the tragic sentiment.” Where else does a darker note sound beneath the cheerful one?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd “seems to be taking the measure of my coffin”; news arrives of the “rascal attack” in Baltimore; the men sing because the more a man sings, “the better he is likely to fight”; the Quaker ladies pray that the country be saved from blood “unless blood must be shed to preserve Law and Liberty.”
Each dark note is lightly made, often as a joke, and the passage ends in fair weather. Students can discuss whether the lightness is courage, youth, or a way of not thinking about what lies ahead.
evidence: seems to be taking the measure of my coffin
underlying all was the tragic sentiment that we might have tragic work presently to do
unless blood must be shed to preserve Law and Liberty

questions.prompt: What “grand fact” does the march teach Winthrop, and how does he say he learned it? Does the rest of the passage support it?
facilitatorNotes: That “our great city was with us as one man, utterly united in the great cause.” He learned it “by two senses”: hundreds of thousands roared it, and thousands slapped it onto his knapsack. Jersey City, the New Jersey line, an Irish shopkeeper and two Quaker ladies add more witnesses.

A cheering crowd in the first week of a four-year war proves enthusiasm more than unity, and Winthrop himself calls the Seventh a sign of the loyalty of the city’s “conservative” class. Accept answers that weigh the evidence either way.
evidence: our great city was with us as one man
This grand fact I learned by two senses.

questions.prompt: Winthrop was killed less than two months after this march. Does knowing that change how you hear “It was worth a life, that march” or “if I live to breakfast again”? Should it?
facilitatorNotes: When he wrote them, the phrases were cheerful exaggeration: the march was an experience worth a lifetime, and the breakfast line is a joke about hungry soldiers. Read now, they seem to foretell his death.

Some readers think a text should be read as its writer meant it, so the essay’s value is its unknowing high spirits; others think the irony is exactly why it belongs on Memorial Day, which remembers such people one by one. Both can cite the passage’s mix of jokes and “tragic sentiment.”
evidence: It was worth a life, that march.
I hope, if I live to breakfast again in the Lapierre House

readings.title: Colonialism in the United States: independence declared, and independence of mind
readings.author: Henry Cabot Lodge
readings.challenge: Find Lodge’s thesis and the two stages of independence he describes. Then decide whether his evidence, Franklin above all, persuades you.
readings.focus: A historian argues that declaring independence in 1776 was the quick part: Americans took much longer to stop thinking like colonists.
readings.context: Henry Cabot Lodge (1850–1924), a Boston historian who later served more than thirty years as a United States senator from Massachusetts, published this essay in the Atlantic Monthly in May 1883; reprinting it in 1914, he added a note that the colonial spirit had since weakened. A colony is a settlement ruled from a mother country; provincial means narrow, small-town. England recognized American independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783); George III was the British king. Spain’s Christian kingdoms fought the Moors, Muslim rulers of much of Spain, for centuries; the Puritans ruled England in the 1650s; the Saxon invasion is the settlement of England by Germanic peoples in the 400s. Lodge’s talk of an “English race” reflects a theory of inherited national character common in his day. It is read on Independence Day because it asks what declaring independence did, and did not, change.
readings.contentNote: Lodge generalizes about whole peoples (Spaniards, South Americans, the French, the “English race”) in ways now recognized as stereotypes.

excerpt.locator: Colonialism in the United States, the opening paragraphs, through the colonists’ “habit of mental dependence”; opens “Nothing is more interesting than to trace, through many years and almost endless…”; closes “…breaking out now here, now there, have at last brought it so near to final extinction.”.

questions.prompt: What “habit of thought” does Lodge set out to trace, and how does the image of the river that disappears underground explain his method?
facilitatorNotes: He will trace “the colonial spirit in our modes of thought,” a habit of looking to England that outlived political dependence. Like a river that vanishes underground and resurfaces “with new shapes and colors,” an idea can seem to disappear and come back looking unrelated, yet “it is always the same river.”
So he will link opinions that seem “sporadic and independent” into one family with “a common ancestor.” Ask whether this is a strength of the essay or a way of making any resemblance count as proof.
evidence: it is always the same river
They all have the same pedigree

questions.prompt: Lodge says armed revolution is quick. What was the harder and slower part of becoming independent, and how does he explain the slowness?
facilitatorNotes: The war took a few years, from 1776 to the victory of 1782 and a government by 1789. The “second stage in the conflict” was “that of ideas and opinions”: Americans kept English law and government, wisely in his view, but also kept a colonial dependence in books, art, learning, fashion and manners.
He blames the “slow mind and ingrained conservatism of the English race.” Students should see that this explanation rests on a theory of inherited national character, which is weak as evidence.
evidence: Armed revolution is quick.
We then entered upon the second stage in the conflict, that of ideas and opinions.

questions.prompt: Why does Lodge prefer the word “colonial” to “provincial,” and how does he define a colony?
facilitatorNotes: “Provincial” has become a vague insult for anything we dislike; “colonial” has historical point and can be defined exactly: a colony is “an off-shoot from a parent stock, and its chief characteristic is dependence.” The less dependent it becomes, the nearer it comes to “national existence.”
The definition lets him measure independence by degrees rather than by a single date. Ask what his list of dependencies includes: goods, politics, books, colleges, professions, fashions, manners.
evidence: its chief characteristic is dependence
When we sought to originate, we simply imitated.

questions.prompt: Lodge calls Franklin the “one great exception” and his autobiography “the corner-stone” of American literature. What makes Franklin “genuinely and intensely American” to him? Does one exception support his case or weaken it?
facilitatorNotes: Franklin’s “audacity,” “fertility” and “adaptability,” his ease before “kings and princes,” and the Autobiography’s “perfect originality,” free of “English colonialism.” Like lightning that shows how dark the storm is, the exception shows how colonial everyone else was.

Franklin’s Autobiography is among this level’s calendar readings, so students can test the claim against the book itself. Some will argue one brilliant exception proves little about a whole people; others that Lodge uses it fairly as a measure. On Independence Day, ask what an independent mind would look like now.
evidence: the luminous genius of Franklin
It is American in feeling, without any taint of English colonialism.
